C-WORKFLOW-PLAN-INDEPENDENCE.Summary: Make delegated execution independent of plan documents, support controller-defined review obligations, and honor explicitly delegated autonomy without losing bounded recovery or truthful acceptance.
C-WORKFLOW-PLAN-INDEPENDENCE.Problem: Standalone delegated tasks can run without a plan, but checkpoint registration and run state require a native approved spec/plan pair. General controller and skill instructions still impose native document and approval ceremonies outside their intended pipeline. Recovery authorization after ordinary allowances requires a user message newer than the stop, so a prior instruction to finish autonomously cannot authorize later bounded continuation.

Goals.Goal: Support native packages, arbitrary provided plans, and conversation-scoped work through the same execution capabilities rather than separate enforcement or bypass paths.
Keep delegated as a division of labor: the controller reasons, coordinates, and accepts; implementation workers edit, test, and fix.
Let the controller assign review obligations when the request or its source does not prescribe them, and mechanically enforce those obligations once assigned.
Honor requests for no spec/plan files and for autonomous completion within explicitly delegated authority, including reasonable reversible decisions and finite recovery.
Keep native vv-spec, vv-plan, and vv-execute useful specialized tools without making them prerequisites for unrelated work.
Simplify conflicting instructions and preserve established verification, permissions, recovery history, and user-reserved stopping points.

Constraints.Constraint: Execution ownership, source of requirements, and delegated authority are distinct concerns. Neither the orchestration profile nor a generic request to implement implies selection of the native spec-to-code pipeline.

Use the existing work-item, acceptance, checkpoint, snapshot, and recovery mechanisms as the foundation. Prefer additive tool inputs or actions over a parallel workflow engine or a new file-based planning language.
The common execution contract validates identities, scopes, dependencies, obligations, results, and budgets; native XML parsing and native lifecycle validation belong to the native input path only.
No catalog of external planning tools, framework-specific prompt exceptions, or native-format conversion requirement. Shipped instructions use generic source terminology.
Preserve explicit identifiers and deterministic counters. Do not infer work-item identity, approval, or loop similarity from embeddings, fuzzy text comparison, or semantic clustering.

Retain ordinary two-attempt delegated and two-generation checkpoint budgets and existing bounded recovery. Add a separately recorded, finite execution-scoped advance-authorization reserve; do not weaken post-stop authorization validation to make older messages pass that unrelated path.

The proposed initial advance-authorization reserve is three additional recovery units shared by the entire authorized execution, not three per task. Each unit grants one implementation attempt or one checkpoint review generation after existing allowances are exhausted. Registering the same authority again cannot refill it.

A recovery still requires diagnosis, a changed condition or approach, and relevant verification. Exhausted budgets suspend the affected automation; neither delegated authority nor changed source labels permit unlimited retries, acceptance of a failed result, or omission of registered review obligations.

Only an eligible root-user instruction can establish or extend autonomous authority. Runtime verifies observable identity, owning session, scope binding, and replay protection; the controller interprets intent. Plan contents, worker output, and generated summaries cannot grant authority.

Autonomy delegates decisions within the task; it does not override host permissions, explicit project constraints, user-reserved approvals, or separately restricted external, destructive, publication, and credential operations. A request to prepare a design is not permission to implement it.

Do not describe delegated approval as personal human review. Native lifecycle transitions under advance authority must retain truthful approval provenance without requiring the user to inspect each generated intermediate document.

Persist execution history, registered obligations, and consumed authority durably even when the source plan is ephemeral. Do not require a repository plan or handoff file merely to retain runtime state.

Existing accepted work, failed reviews, recovery histories, and native source checks remain meaningful across supported snapshot upgrades. Invalid state fails with diagnostics rather than resetting progress or granting authority.

Use synthetic fixtures and generic product descriptions in all artifacts, tests, documentation, comments, and publication inputs. Keep raw conversations and unrelated project information out of repository content.
Do not change model-role assignments, presets, host permissions, active user configuration, or installed global skills. Preserve the existing install/sync/restart model.

NonGoals.NonGoal: No removal of runtime tracking, assigned reviewer gates, finite correction budgets, or evidence-based controller acceptance.

No mandatory final spec/code reviewer pair or mandatory intermediate checkpoint for provided-plan and conversation-scoped executions. Native package obligations remain those declared by the selected native package.
No built-in parser or dedicated integration for each external plan format; no rewriting external source documents into native packages.

No universal proof that a controller extracted every requirement from arbitrary prose or chose every necessary review. Runtime enforces registered obligations; semantic completeness remains an agent responsibility.
No new scheduler, recursive delegation, automatic model escalation, cross-session run adoption, provider retry engine, or host timeout redesign.
No new evaluation platform, model benchmark, mandatory user journal, or large catalog of prompt rules.
No redesign of unrelated plugins, release automation, public package exports, or canonical vvoc configuration. No changes to archived lifecycle bundles.

No requirement to refactor native XML syntax or add an alternative native approval status. Preserve existing native artifact compatibility and represent additional provenance through the execution contract or existing explanatory fields where appropriate.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: AC-01: A delegated request can begin and complete without a spec file, a plan file, a native package directory, or a new approval ceremony introduced solely by vvoc. It still uses bounded worker assignments and explicit controller acceptance; no independent review is fabricated or silently required when none is assigned.

AC-02: Native-package, provided-plan, and conversation-scoped inputs use one common execution model. The generic path does not require native plan/spec paths, native lifecycle statuses, XML element names, or a predeclared complete wave list. A small request does not require a multi-document or multi-stage setup.

AC-03: The native path retains automatic obligation extraction, strict artifact validation, source-hash binding, and native checkpoint coverage. A failure on a selected native package does not silently fall back to generic execution with weaker obligations. Existing native runs retain their source mode and requirements.

AC-04: A provided plan remains its original source of requirements and lifecycle rules. The controller supplies task contracts and review obligations through generic runtime operations; no native copy, external-factory name, special parser, or second lifecycle is required. Runtime does not interpret source text as executable commands or authorization.

AC-05: Conversation-scoped execution supports starting with one task, batch-registering known work, and explicitly adding dependency-ready tasks or checkpoints as understanding develops. Additions are checked for valid references, acyclic dependencies, scope, and consistency with current execution state. They do not restart accepted tasks or reopen a sealed execution implicitly.

AC-06: Required reviews come from the selected source, an explicit user instruction, or a controller decision. The controller can request a standalone review or bind an independent review checkpoint to one or more work items without a plan file. The canonical requiredReviewers concept remains usable and clearly distinguished from per-task acceptance and group checkpoint coverage.

AC-07: With no source-prescribed reviewers, the controller may select no independent review, code review, spec review, or both according to the task. Runtime does not install a universal final-review default. Spec review checks the request and acceptance criteria and does not require a physical specification document.

AC-08: Once an implementation review obligation is registered, the dependent barrier and completion checks require its actual applicable results. Controller acceptance, a closed review-only FAIL report, an empty list, or an authority grant cannot satisfy it. Existing compatible reviewer results may be bound by exact identity and snapshot rather than duplicated; a prose claim that review occurred is insufficient.

AC-09: Registered requirements and review obligations cannot be silently removed, reclassified as optional, or invalidated by source switching to finish after a failure. Any supported amendment preserves provenance and affected review history. Replacing or splitting existing work through runtime operations preserves explicit lineage and consumed recovery budget; no semantic guessing is introduced.

AC-10: Generic completion checks all registered work and assigned barriers without requiring a nonexistent final checkpoint. When a final checkpoint was assigned, completion requires its current coverage of the result it claims to review. Work added or changed after review does not inherit stale approval. No-review completion is represented honestly as controller-accepted, not independently reviewed.

AC-11: Explicit autonomous authority may be established before a future stop and remains usable for the authorized execution. It records its root-user provenance, execution and scope boundary, delegated stages, reserved stopping points, and finite recovery reserve. Creating it requires no extra user question when the initiating instruction already supplies that authority.

AC-12: Advance authority permits the controller to make reasonable implementation decisions and, for a bounded prototype or experiment, reversible product and UX choices within the requested goal. Material decisions are disclosed without converting each disclosure into a blocking question. Explicit instructions to stop at a finished specification, prepared plan, or before publication remain binding.

AC-13: The native skills may progress through the stages explicitly delegated by the user after their own required checks, without demanding another manual approval merely because a document was generated later. Human-reserved gates still wait. Lifecycle and result records distinguish controller action under delegated authority from personal user review; no fabricated approval or passing verification is recorded.

AC-14: The three-unit advance recovery reserve is shared across the authorized execution and consumed once per extra attempt or generation. Ordinary allowances and existing rework/recovery do not replenish it. Duplicate calls, concurrent grants, target replacement, restart, and replay of the originating message cannot increase the reserve. Further extension requires a new explicit authorization, never controller self-renewal.

AC-15: Advance authority can be narrowed or revoked without undoing historical work. Already consumed units remain consumed; later recovery cannot use revoked or foreign authority. Unavailable or invalid provenance denies only the proposed authority or extension and must not be reported as successful approval.

AC-16: BLOCKED, NEEDS_CONTEXT, report rejection, and budget exhaustion remain distinct from success. The controller diagnoses the affected work and uses an authorized bounded path when available, including advance authority, instead of unnecessarily waiting for a newer user message. Without an authorized safe path it reports the actual limitation and partial result; it does not loop indefinitely or claim completion.

AC-17: Generic and native execution state, dynamic obligations, lineage, approval provenance, reserve consumption, and recovery results persist atomically. Persistence failure must not expose unrecorded acceptance or additional launch authority. Supported old snapshots load without invented advance permissions, reviewers, or lost history, and ephemeral source plans do not imply ephemeral counters.

AC-18: Controller, orchestration, workflow guidance, and native skill descriptions consistently separate work ownership, source, and autonomy. Replace universal native-document prerequisites and unconditional manual stage transitions with source- and authority-specific rules. A request for no files, no subagents, or no intermediate questions is interpreted independently rather than conflated.

AC-19: vv-spec, vv-plan, and vv-execute remain specialized native-package tools. Their discovery descriptions no longer instruct invocation before every implementation or any arbitrary plan. If another execution procedure is selected, vvoc does not superimpose native planning requirements; generic workflow capabilities remain available without disguising managed agent identities.

AC-20: Simplify interview and execution instructions by removing exhaustive decision-tree mandates, redundant approval questions, repeated ceremonial narration, and automatic blocker-to-handoff behavior. Preserve sufficient contract/consumer investigation, practical verification, assigned reviews, and clear user-requested dialogue. Review-only and discussion-only requests remain findings or discussion rather than unintended implementation.

AC-21: Shipped prompts and skills use generic native-package, provided-plan, and conversation-scoped terminology rather than listing external planning tools. Documentation distinguishes mechanical enforcement of registered obligations from model judgment about completeness and review selection, and explains authority limits and restart behavior without promising uninterrupted or error-free execution.

AC-22: Deterministic tests exercise all three input paths through completion, dynamic review assignment with no source file, rejection of skipped or stale required review, valid no-review completion, incremental tasks, source-switch and grant-replay rejection, advance authority predating a stop, shared-reserve exhaustion, revocation, persistence failure, and compatibility with existing native and legacy work items.

AC-23: Instruction delivery tests and a focused scenario audit cover no-document implementation, delegated preparation with a reserved final approval, fully delegated native progression, reversible prototype decisions, explicit publication exclusion, and discussion-only requests. These checks must not be represented as measured model effectiveness; a bounded sandbox smoke run can supplement them without introducing an evaluation platform.

AC-24: README and the owning context, graph, verification, contracts, and tests are reconciled within the approved implementation lifecycle. Before implementation the derived plan must exercise its actual behavior-sensitive baselines, not treat successful draft grammar validation as proof that the baseline matches the repository.

VerificationIntent.ExpectedEvidence: SDK-shaped integration scenarios verify reachable execution and retained guards, not just successful registration. Permission and authority counterexamples verify no unintended broadening. Native artifact tests verify unchanged syntax and input-specific validation. One final independent spec/code review evaluates the implementation and coordinated instructions. All fixtures and descriptions are synthetic; prompt audit and deterministic tests alone do not demonstrate improved real-model behavior.

Assumptions.Assumption: Three shared additional recovery units is a proposed initial default for explicitly autonomous execution, not a benchmark-derived optimum. It is presented for specification approval rather than silently selected during implementation.
The generic execution contract is runtime bookkeeping, not a replacement plan document or another approval authority. It may record source references and scoped authorization without requiring files.

Source and intent interpretation remain controller responsibilities. Runtime validates explicit data and trusted provenance and does not claim to understand arbitrary external formats or natural-language approval.

Precise additive tool signatures, the internal execution-state representation, and a backward-readable persistence version are implementation-plan decisions. They must satisfy the behavior above without introducing framework-specific adapters or new mandatory user setup.

The requested deliverable at this stage is a draft specification and explanatory design context only. Approval of this draft and an implementation plan precede source changes; no implementation, commit, installation, or release is performed as part of specification authoring.
